Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘Juzhi's one finger.’ The phrase occurs 87 times in 47 allowlisted texts and names Juzhi's recorded response of raising one finger. The Lamp Record supplies the narrative behind the label: Tianlong showed Juzhi one raised finger; thereafter Juzhi raised one finger to visiting monks; when a boy copied him, Juzhi cut off the boy's finger, called him back, and raised his own finger. Later records place ‘Juzhi's one finger’ beside Xuefeng's rolling ball, Yunmen's looking-and-‘look!,’ Muzhou's ‘ready-made,’ Deshan's staff, and Linji's shout as a named response associated with a master. Verses call it ‘one-finger Chan,’ say it was used throughout Juzhi's life, and repeatedly ask or comment on where he was accurate. The entry reports the gesture, its narrative, and its later case-label use; the texts do not supply a further gloss for what the finger denotes.
Senses.Note: Zen bends an ordinary finger into the stable name of Juzhi's public response and case. The headword is the case/device label, not a separate body-part sense. Cross-check with ‘one-finger Chan’ (一指頭禪): that compound names the same recorded device, so no second sense is created here. The underlying Lamp Record narrative is attested in T51n2076 even though its wording does not use the compact headword.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A collected verse says: ‘report that the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the west lies only on Juzhi's one fingertip.’ This is quoted as the verse's wording, not adopted as a definition.

Senses.PreferredTarget: walk on the deepest ocean floor
AlternateTargets: go at the very bottom of the sea
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “walk at the deep-deep bottom of the sea.” In 205 occurrences across 116 allowlisted texts, it overwhelmingly forms the second half of the paired formula “stand on the highest peak; walk on the deepest ocean floor” (高高峰頂立，深深海底行). The pair is spoken as advice, posed as a public question—“how do you understand it?” (汝作麼生會)—and reused in later appraisal and comment. One record pairs two people, “one stands on the high-high mountaintop; one walks at the deep-deep bottom of the sea” (一人高高山頂立，一人深深海底行); another expands the parallel with “one sails a boat on the mountain; one races a horse before the cliff” (一個山上行船，一個巖前走馬). Yuanwu answers the quoted pair with “a staff strikes a stone man’s head” (棒打石人頭). The phrase’s Chan deviation is this stable, publicly tested two-line formula, not an ordinary report of underwater travel.
Senses.Note: The mountain and sea halves are one paired formula, not separate senses. Different replies to the same interview line are readings or responses, not different referents.
